strengths: Novel and genuinely interesting reformulation: casting genomic modeling as OCR-style document understanding is a fresh perspective that departs from the dominant 1D token-sequence paradigm, and the mapping of OCR primitives (reading, grounding, retrieval, completion) to genomic operations (transcription, variant localization, subsequence search, imputation) is conceptually appealing.

Strong headline result on a standard, externally defined benchmark: on DNALONGBENCH eQTL prediction, OpticalDNA reaches 0.852 AUROC with a 256K-parameter linear probe and 0.867 with a shallow MLP, outperforming HyenaDNA, Caduceus-Ph, JanusDNA, and the 252M-parameter Expert Model (Table 2), with gains concentrated on hard tissues (WB, Thyroid).

Extensive experimentation and documentation: three downstream benchmarks, six pretraining tasks (T1-T6) with per-task evaluations (Tables S22-S27), a rendering-resolution efficiency study (Table 7), Grad-CAM interpretability, and a detailed appendix covering rendering, prompt contracts, hyperparameters, and benchmark construction.

Commendable transparency about weak results: the paper reports poor T5 grounding (Det-Acc 0.0055 at IoU=0.99), near-chance T6 chromosome classification (0.062/0.104 accuracy over ~24 classes), and low T4 masked-completion EM (~0.13), rather than hiding them.

The efficiency direction is practically motivated and, at the level of the trained probe, adaptation is cheap (256K-2.3M trainable parameters), and the whole-genome inference time of 12.3 minutes is a concrete practical advantage.
weaknesses: Central efficiency claims are misleading. The abstract and contributions state OpticalDNA surpasses models with 'up to 985× more activated parameters while tuning only 256k trainable parameters,' but 985× is 252M/256K, i.e., it compares the expert model's activated parameters to OpticalDNA's trainable probe size. At inference OpticalDNA still runs a ~400M-parameter frozen encoder (SAM-Conv-CLIP-L 389.8M + projector + fusion). 'Activated' and 'trainable' parameters are conflated, which materially overstates the efficiency contribution.

The '~20× fewer effective tokens' claim is framed as a compute saving, but the compression ratio (Table 7) is nucleotides-per-visual-token, not a like-for-like compute measure. Encoding a 640×640 page through a vision backbone is far more expensive than reading ~20 sequence tokens, so token-count reduction does not translate into the claimed computational advantage.

The paper's thesis (OCR-style 'understanding') is undermined by its own task results: T5 grounding is essentially failing (Det-Acc 0.0055-0.0462), T6 chromosome classification is near random (0.062 vs. ~0.042 chance), and T4 masked completion has ~13% EM. If the core 'genomic understanding' primitives largely fail, the framing that region-aware OCR understanding is the key to genomic modeling is not well supported.

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair. Evo-2 and LucaOne are used as frozen feature extractors with a single linear head (Appendix G.2), and Evo-2 is truncated to 70,000-base fragments due to single-H100 limits rather than its native million-token context; this likely understates their capability, so the RiceSubBench/RiceWGPB advantages may be partly an artifact of adaptation budget rather than representation quality.

RiceWGPB results rest on very small samples (102 and 130 accessions; 21 and 26 test points) with tiny RMSE differences (2.952 vs 3.056 for TGW; 9.531 vs 9.617 for LRI-15SZ), which may not be statistically meaningful, and RiceSubBench/RiceWGPB are new in-house benchmarks without external validation, limiting comparability.

The ablation (Section 4.3, Fig. 3) only compares against the DeepSeek-OCR backbone, so it does not isolate which of the proposed ingredients (rendering, six tasks, multi-page fusion, two-stage adaptation) drive gains; the marginal +5.37% average over the backbone, combined with near-chance baselines on rice (Evo-2/LucaOne ~0.49-0.55 accuracy), suggests the underlying tasks may be weak discriminators.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: no code/data release is mentioned, and reproducing the full pipeline requires ~11 days on 8×H100 plus a two-stage schedule; the model is derived from DeepSeek-OCR, whose licensing for this use is not discussed.

strengths: The core idea—reframing genomic sequence modeling as OCR-style document understanding—is genuinely novel and creatively connects document-analysis primitives (reading, grounding, retrieval, completion) to genomic operations. The mapping is conceptually interesting even if the execution is problematic.

The manuscript is unusually thorough in its task design and documentation: Appendix B-D specify six task protocols, response contracts, rendering geometry, and bounding-box annotation schemes in reproducible detail, and Appendix E-G provide pretraining/downstream hyperparameters.

The rice cross-subspecies results (Table 3) and the long-context eQTL improvements over JanusDNA (Table 2) show consistent gains over prior sequence baselines, and the multi-page fusion design (Section 3.4) is a reasonable way to make a vision backbone length-invariant.
weaknesses: The central claim is undermined by the authors' own ablation. Table S21 shows that the DNA-agnostic DeepSeek-OCR backbone alone reaches 0.823 average AUROC on DNALONGBENCH eQTL, versus 0.867 for OpticalDNA and 0.791 for JanusDNA. In other words, an off-the-shelf OCR model that was never trained on DNA already surpasses every sequence baseline the paper competes against, and the proposed DNA-specific formulation adds only +5.37%. This strongly suggests the reported gains come from the vision modality / model scale rather than the proposed OCR-style pretraining, which is precisely the contribution claimed.

Efficiency and parameter claims are misleading. The abstract headline 'surpasses models with up to 985× more activated parameters while tuning only 256k trainable parameters' compares a 256K-parameter linear probe head against fully trained models (e.g., Enformer's 252M). The representation being probed was produced by a frozen SAM-Conv-CLIP-L encoder (~389M) plus a 3B MoE decoder, so the '256K' number describes only the downstream head, not the model that learned the representation. This is an apples-to-oranges framing that inflates the efficiency contribution.

The 'compression' claim is not substantiated and is likely illusory. A page holds ~1800 nucleotides but is a 640×640 image partitioned into 16×16 patches (≈1600 patches/page) processed by a heavy CLIP/SAM front-end. Replacing ~1800 nucleotide tokens with ~1600 visual patches plus a large vision encoder is not obviously cheaper compute; the paper reports no direct FLOPs or wall-clock comparison against a sequence transformer of comparable scale. The 'nearly 20× fewer effective tokens' and 'compression ratio' figures (Table 7) are defined only relative to visual token counts and never tied to actual compute.

Half of the proposed task suite is essentially non-functional, contradicting the framing that these primitives 'naturally correspond' to practical genomic workflows. T5 (subsequence localization) yields Det-Acc@IoU=0.5 of 0.0462 on HG38 and 0.6800 on rice with Both-Acc 0.024/0.393 (Table S24); T6 (chromosome classification) reaches 0.062/0.104 accuracy, barely above chance over 24 classes (Table S27); T4 (mask completion) achieves Text-EM 0.13 and Text-CER 0.58 (Table S25). These failures are acknowledged only briefly and are not reflected in the abstract's claims.

The controlled 1D-vs-2D comparison used to justify the 2D document representation (Appendix A) is not a fair test of modality. It pits a hand-built 1D CNN family against strong off-the-shelf TIMM 2D backbones (MobileNetV3, TinyNet, ResNet-10t). The 1D family is clearly under-optimized—CNN1D-large (0.553) is worse than CNN1D-small (0.649)—so the '2D CNNs win' conclusion reflects architecture/optimization quality, not the superiority of rendering DNA as images.

Baseline comparisons are confounded and in places unfair. Evo-2 is chunked at 70,000 bp rather than its intended long context 'because the original million-token inference depends on multi-GPU implementations,' directly handicapping the strongest long-context competitor, and all baselines are frozen-feature + linear-head while OpticalDNA's features come from a much larger pretrained stack. RiceWGPB (Table 4) uses test sets of only 21 and 26 samples, so RMSE differences (e.g., TGW 2.952 vs 3.056) are well within noise and cannot support the efficiency/practicality claims.

Comparisons conflate modality with model scale and pretraining data. OpticalDNA's encoder+decoder is a multi-billion-parameter vision-language stack; the sequence baselines (HyenaDNA 1.6M, Caduceus 7.7M) are orders of magnitude smaller. Attributing the gains to the OCR reformulation is not supported when the comparison simultaneously varies scale, pretraining corpus, and modality.

Internal inconsistencies and presentation errors reduce confidence. The parameter count '409M' does not match the described 389M encoder + 570M activated decoder; Figure 3's legend and caption say 'VisualDNA'; Table S26 labels a setting 'OpticalDNA-Rice-HG38'; Appendix D repeatedly writes 'morbidity' where 'verbosity' is intended; NUMIMAGES/NUM_IMAGES and 'Max text tokens'/'T_max' are used inconsistently. Equation (S12) describes Det-IoU(avg) with a threshold clause that contradicts the following text.

Reproducibility is limited: training requires 8×H100 for ~8+3 days (HG38) plus ~5 days (rice), depends on the DeepSeek-OCR base model and a specific rendering/annotation pipeline, and there is no released code/weights or independent verification of the rendering-annotation alignment. There is also an unaddressed data-leakage concern: pretraining on HG38 and evaluating human eQTL tasks derived from the same reference genome.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and original reformulation of genomic modeling as OCR-style document understanding, with a vision-based DNA foundation model and a well-specified suite of six prompt-conditioned tasks.

Provides extensive experiments across human eQTL (DNALONGBench), rice subspecies generalization, and rice whole-genome phenotype prediction, with detailed appendices covering hyperparameters, task construction, metrics, and baselines.

The eQTL results are strong in places: OpticalDNA achieves 0.867 average AUROC with an MLP probe and 0.852 with linear probing, outperforming JanusDNA and other baselines on several tissues while using lightweight downstream heads.

The rice subspecies OOD results show promising transfer across distribution shifts, with accuracy gains over Evo-2 and LucaOne, and the wall-clock inference time for a 390M-base genome (12.3 minutes) is practically attractive.
The paper is generally well-organized, with a clear description of the rendering pipeline, visual encoder, document decoder, and prompt-conditioned pretraining objectives.
weaknesses: Several core OCR-style primitives are not actually learned: T5 subsequence localization is near zero under strict grounding (Det-Acc@IoU=0.99 is 0.0055 for HG38 and 0.0623 for rice; Both-Acc is 0.0037 and 0.0605), T4 masked completion has Text-EM around 0.13 and Strict around 0.05, and T6 chromosome classification is near chance (0.062 for HG38 with 24 classes; 0.104 for rice with 12 classes). This directly contradicts the claimed learning of retrieval, completion, and global understanding.

The efficiency claims are misleading. The abstract and introduction claim '985x fewer activated parameters' by comparing a 256K linear probe to a 252M expert model, but the frozen visual encoder alone is approximately 398M parameters, and the rice table lists OpticalDNA as 409M activated parameters. The '20x fewer effective tokens' claim counts only decoder-side visual tokens and ignores the large visual encoder compute over roughly 1600 patches per page. The paper conflates trainable and activated parameters.

The whole-genome phenotype results are weak and do not beat trivial baselines. For TGW, the reported RMSE of 2.952 exceeds the label standard deviation of 2.84 (i.e., worse than predicting the mean). For LRI-15SZ, RMSE 9.531 is worse than the mean predictor (std 6.77) and worse than a zero predictor (roughly 7.27). The dataset is tiny (102/130 samples), improvements over Evo-2 are marginal, and no significance tests or trivial baselines are reported.

There is no fair comparison to sequence-based models with equivalent compression or pretraining budget. The 1D vs. 2D CNN comparison in Figure 1c is trained from scratch for 10 epochs and does not represent modern genomic foundation models; the ablation against DeepSeek-OCR only isolates DNA-specific pretraining rather than vision versus sequence processing.

The model is pretrained only on 2048-bp windows, yet the paper claims long-context modeling up to 450k bases. The multi-page fusion module is trained on roughly two pages, not hundreds, so the long-context mechanism is not actually validated or learned during pretraining. Downstream evaluation relies on mean-pooling many pages that the fusion module never saw during training.

The 'selective, understanding-driven compression' claim is unsupported. The visual encoder processes all patches uniformly, compression is fixed by rendering resolution and patch size, and there is no explicit region-selective or jump-based mechanism. The 2D layout is simply wrapped text and does not inherently encode sparse genomic structure or long-range regulatory interactions.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations section, does not release code or model weights, and requires very heavy compute (8xH100 for 8+3 days for HG38 and 5 days for rice), limiting reproducibility despite detailed appendices.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence: OpticalDNA does not 'consistently outperform' baselines on all tissues (e.g., NT and SSELL are better with JanusDNA MLP), and naming/writing inconsistencies (e.g., 'VisualDNA' in Figure 3, 'morbidity' for verbosity in the appendix) reduce clarity.

strengths: Novel and creative framing: reformulating genomic modeling as OCR-style document understanding is an unusual and thought-provoking direction that connects two previously separate fields (document VLM understanding and genomic foundation models).

Strong empirical results on the DNALONGBENCH eQTL benchmark, achieving SOTA average AUROC (0.852 with linear probe, 0.867 with MLP) and outperforming prior SOTA JanusDNA across all nine GTEx tissues, with consistent gains on harder tissues (WB, Thyroid).

The cross-species transfer analysis (Appendix O.1) is a genuinely valuable control: OpticalDNA-HG38 outperforms HG38-pretrained Caduceus and JanusDNA on RiceSubBench, partially disentangling the effect of the visual formulation from domain-matched rice pretraining.

Controlled 1D vs. 2D comparisons (Appendix A) are a reasonable attempt to isolate the representation effect, including a matched-token-budget/shared-backbone experiment (Table S5: 2D 0.626 vs 1D 0.558) that controls for token compression and backbone differences.

Thorough and honest reproducibility and contamination analyses: strict 100% full-sequence overlap criterion, k-mer containment analysis (Table S26) showing partial overlap does not induce label consistency, and explicit generalization-beyond-memorization discussion.
Extensive supplementary documentation of tasks, prompts, hyperparameters, and evaluation protocols, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The headline efficiency claim is misleading. 'Tuning only 256k trainable parameters' and '985× fewer activated parameters' compare OpticalDNA's tiny linear probe (256K) against Enformer's total/activated parameters (252M). OpticalDNA itself activates ~409M parameters at inference (Table S36) and is built on a large pretrained DeepSeek-OCR backbone. Comparing trainable probe parameters to a model's total parameters is an apples-to-oranges comparison that inflates the efficiency story.

The critical comparison is with the backbone itself (DeepSeek-OCR), which is buried in the ablation (Fig. 3) and shows only +5.37% relative average gain. This suggests that much of the downstream performance comes from the pretrained VLM backbone rather than the proposed OCR-style DNA formulation, and the paper does not convincingly isolate the DNA-specific contribution in the main results.

Four of the six claimed 'core genomic primitives' perform poorly: T4 masked completion (Text-EM ≈ 0.13, Strict ≈ 0.05), T5 subsequence localization (Det-Acc ≈ 0.005–0.06 at IoU=0.99, Both-Acc ≈ 0.003–0.06), and T6 chromosome classification (0.062 HG38, 0.104 rice, near the ~0.042 chance level). This undercuts the claim of learning 'layout-aware DNA representations that retain fine-grained genomic information.'

The biological motivation is questionable and largely conceded in Appendix B: rendering is a lossless bijection, so the claim that it 'converts discontinuous long-range dependencies into spatial structure' is not substantiated—rasterizing a sequence into rows does not change long-range dependency structure, only re-indexes positions. The paper acknowledges it is a 'computational' rather than 'biological' reformulation, but the introduction's 'structure-aware reading' framing overstates this.

Baseline comparisons on long-context tasks are partly unfair: NT-v2-500M and GENERator-1.2B do not natively support 450 kb inputs and are evaluated via chunking with frozen backbones and linear probes, which discards long-range information that OpticalDNA's multi-page fusion can exploit.

The interpretability analysis (Grad-CAM, Fig. 4 and S4–S5) is purely qualitative and based on two examples, which is thin evidence for the claim that the model 'localizes biologically meaningful splice signals' and prioritizes relevant pages.

Pretraining cost is very high (~88 H100-days for HG38 plus 5 days for rice), and the evaluation relies on 'best validation score' reporting with tiny probing heads, making it unclear how robust the reported gains are to head/hyperparameter choices.

strengths: The paper presents an original and creative reformulation of genomic modeling as an OCR-style document understanding problem, which is a novel angle compared to mainstream sequence-based approaches.
The idea of rendering DNA sequences into multi-page images and leveraging vision-language models with OCR-inspired tasks is conceptually interesting and potentially opens a new research direction.
The paper includes extensive appendix material with detailed task definitions, hyperparameters, and additional experiments, demonstrating a significant amount of work.
weaknesses: The central claim that 2D visual modeling outperforms 1D sequential modeling for long-context genomics is not convincingly supported. The main comparison in Table 2 is misleading: OpticalDNA is evaluated with a frozen 409M-parameter encoder and only a 256K-parameter linear probe, while baselines like JanusDNA and NT-v2-500M are fully fine-tuned or have many more trainable parameters. The paper emphasizes '985x fewer activated parameters' but ignores the large frozen encoder, which still requires substantial computation. This is an unfair comparison that inflates the perceived efficiency.

The efficiency claims are exaggerated and confusing. The abstract states 'nearly 20x fewer effective tokens' but the method still processes multi-page 640x640 images (up to hundreds of pages for 450kb sequences), which are computationally expensive. The definition of 'effective tokens' is unclear and appears to be an arbitrary metric that does not reflect actual computational cost. The paper does not provide a fair end-to-end FLOPs or latency comparison against sequence-based models under matched conditions.

The evaluation on DNALONGBENCH is incomplete and weak. The paper only evaluates eQTL tasks, omitting the other tasks in the benchmark (e.g., enhancer, promoter, splice site prediction). More critically, the paper does not report results for OpticalDNA with a 1D sequence representation, making it impossible to isolate whether the gains come from the visual modality or from the pretraining data/setup. The ablation study compares against DeepSeek-OCR, a general OCR model, which is not a meaningful genomic baseline.

The claimed advantage of 2D over 1D is not rigorously established. The controlled comparison in Appendix A uses different model architectures (e.g., TinyNet-E vs. CNN1D) and does not control for pretraining or tokenization. The matched-token-budget experiment (Table S5) uses a fixed 10,000 tokens and a Transformer backbone, but the 1D sequence representation is not defined (e.g., k-mer tokenization?), and the 2D image is only 336x336, which may not reflect the full method. The result (0.626 vs. 0.558) is marginal and could be due to confounding factors.

The biological motivation is questionable. The paper claims that genomic semantics are 'sparse and discontinuous' and that 2D layout helps, but DNA is inherently a 1D sequence, and the rasterization introduces no biological priors (as admitted in Appendix B). The 'structure' is purely computational, but the paper repeatedly implies biological alignment (e.g., 'phrase-like reading behavior'). This overstates the biological relevance and could mislead readers.

The paper is poorly written and contains numerous typographical errors. Examples include: 'morbidity' instead of 'verbosity' in multiple appendices (E.1, E.3, E.6), 'Rethinking' misspelled as 'Rethinking' in the page header, '200K' instead of '256K' in the abstract (Table 2 shows 256K), and inconsistent notation. These errors undermine the paper's credibility and make it difficult to read.

The reproducibility is questionable due to the massive compute required (8x H100 for weeks) and the lack of code or model release. The training details are complex and may not be easily reproducible. The paper does not provide a clear, step-by-step recipe for pretraining or evaluation.

The limitations are not adequately discussed. The paper does not address the fundamental inefficiency of rendering and processing images for long sequences, nor does it discuss the potential loss of information due to rasterization (e.g., line breaks disrupting continuous motifs). The impact statement is generic and does not reflect the specific risks of this method.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel paradigm by reformulating genomic sequence modeling as OCR-style document understanding, with a vision-based DNA foundation model and six prompt-conditioned tasks (T1-T6).

Reports strong results on the standard DNALONGBENCH eQTL benchmark: 0.852 average AUROC with a 256K-parameter linear probe and 0.867 with a lightweight MLP, outperforming JanusDNA MLP (0.840) while tuning far fewer downstream parameters.

Provides extensive experiments across human and rice benchmarks, including a rice subspecies benchmark and a whole-genome phenotype benchmark, with detailed appendices covering hyperparameters, contamination analysis, rendering ablations, and cross-species transfer.
Includes a thoughtful impact statement discussing genomic privacy, data governance, and fairness risks, which is appropriate for genomic foundation models.

Demonstrates efficient adaptation and competitive throughput in some settings, and the controlled 2D-vs-1D comparisons in the appendix, if valid, support the potential of document-style representations.
weaknesses: The efficiency claims are misleading. The abstract states '985x fewer activated parameters,' but 252M / 256K compares Enformer's activated parameters to OpticalDNA's trainable parameters. OpticalDNA actually activates ~408M parameters at inference, more than Enformer's 252M. Similarly, 'nearly 20x fewer effective tokens' is ambiguous: it compares visual tokens before multi-page fusion to base tokens, while the downstream model ultimately uses a fixed L=100 fused document representation; the compression ratio vs. k-mer tokenization is much smaller.

The paper claims OpticalDNA 'consistently outperforms' baselines, but on DNALONGBENCH it does not beat JanusDNA on all tissues (e.g., NT: 0.900 vs. 0.914 for MLP; SSELL: 0.832 vs. 0.846; AT is tied at 0.852). The claim of consistent superiority is overstated.

Baseline comparisons on the rice benchmarks are not fair. Evo-2 and LucaOne are used as frozen feature extractors with severe chunking (70,000 bp for Evo-2, 1,280 bp for LucaOne) and mean pooling, which destroys their long-context capabilities. Their poor performance does not convincingly show that OpticalDNA outperforms these models under comparable conditions.

The central claim that OCR-style visual reformulation is responsible for downstream gains is not fully isolated. The ablation only compares against the general DeepSeek-OCR backbone, so improvements could stem from domain-specific pretraining on HG38/rice rather than from the OCR-style tasks. The matched-token/shared-backbone experiment in Appendix A.4 is poorly described and does not clearly control tokenization, rendering, or training details.

The architecture's long-range modeling is questionable. Multi-page fusion uses one self-attention layer followed by mean reduction over pages, and pretraining uses ~2048-bp windows (about 1-2 pages). At downstream time, the model is applied to 450 kb inputs (226 pages) and potentially whole genomes (~400M bases, hundreds of thousands of pages). How the fusion module generalizes to such extreme page counts is not explained, and the whole-genome inference procedure (12.3 minutes for 400M bases) lacks critical implementation details.

Several OCR-style pretraining tasks perform poorly, undermining the 'understanding' narrative: T6 chromosome classification achieves only 0.062/0.104 accuracy, T5 subsequence localization has strict page success of 0.0037/0.0605, and T4 masked completion has ~0.13 exact match. While these are pretraining probes, the paper does not show that they contribute to downstream gains.

There is no dedicated limitations section in the main paper. Important potential failure modes are not analyzed, such as artificial line breaks creating false local correlations between bases that are far apart in the sequence, or the risk that 2D convolutions exploit rasterization artifacts rather than genuine genomic structure.

Reproducibility is partly limited by the very expensive pretraining protocol (11 days on 8×H100 for HG38 plus 5 days for rice) and the reliance on DeepSeek-OCR components; code and exact data splits for the new rice benchmarks are not clearly released or referenced in the manuscript.
